claims.text: The target material family is Fe-Co-Ni-based face-centered-cubic high-entropy alloys.
The property targeted for improvement is high-temperature strength through precipitation hardening.
The primary scientific challenge is insufficient theoretical understanding of orbital-moment or spin-orbit-coupling contributions to ordered-precipitate stability and dislocation pinning.
Adding elements such as Al, Cr, Ti, or Mn to Fe-Co-Ni-based alloys can produce ordered precipitates.
High-throughput screening and multiscale modeling can accelerate discovery of precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys.
High-throughput screening and multiscale modeling can identify Fe-Co-Ni compositions containing L21 or B2 precipitates in an FCC matrix.
HPHT treatment at 6 GPa and 1473 K is applicable to an Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloy.
HPHT treatment stabilizes L21 or B2 precipitates and refines the microstructure of Fe-Co-Ni-based FCC alloys.
Specific thermal cycling induces order-disorder transitions in the proposed Fe-Co-Ni-based alloys.
L21 or B2 ordered precipitates can occur within the FCC matrix of the target Fe-Co-Ni-based alloys.
Orbital-moment contributions govern ordered-precipitate stability and lattice misfit.
Severe local lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys impedes dislocation motion and strengthens the alloy.
Ordered precipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby enhance strength.
Orbital-moment contributions affect mixing enthalpy, electronic structure, order-disorder transition temperatures, and precipitate coherency.
Incomplete treatment of orbital moments currently limits the predictive accuracy of thermodynamic databases for Fe-Co-Ni-based FCC alloys.
A thermodynamic database incorporating orbital-moment effects will predict stable, high-density ordered precipitates.
The predicted precipitate population will give Fe-Co-Ni-based FCC alloys superior high-temperature strength relative to current ferritic superalloys.
Currently developed ferritic superalloys have inadequate high-temperature strength that limits their use.
Standard Fe-Co-Ni high-entropy alloys have low high-temperature strength and poorly predicted order-disorder transitions.
The cited evidence does not explicitly address orbital-moment contributions in Fe-Co-Ni-based FCC alloys.
